a1-shopping-requests.example: Can I have two apples and a bottle of water, please? How much is it?
a1-shopping-requests.reason: Two apples is a countable quantity. A bottle gives a unit for water. The final question asks the price.
a1-shopping-requests.foundation: A clear shopping request names the item and quantity. Ask one question at a time and check the total before paying.

a1-short-stories.title: Understanding a short story
a1-short-stories.summary: Follow people, events and time in a simple story.
a1-short-stories.goal: Understand the order of events in a short story.
a1-short-stories.explain: Stories often use the past simple for completed events: “She opened the door.” Use time words such as first, then, after that and finally to follow the order. Use was/were + -ing to describe what was in progress when another event happened.
a1-short-stories.contrast: Past simple moves the story forward. Past continuous often gives background: “It was raining when she left.” Pronouns such as he, she and they refer to people already named; check the reference as you read.
a1-short-stories.example: First, Mia missed the bus. Then she called her brother, who picked her up.
a1-short-stories.reason: Missed and called are finished events. Then shows what happened next. Her refers to Mia.
a1-short-stories.foundation: To understand a story, identify who is involved, what happened and in what order. Time words and pronouns help connect the events.

a1-some-any-quantities.title: Some, any and quantities
a1-some-any-quantities.summary: Talk about amounts in offers, questions and negatives.
a1-some-any-quantities.goal: Choose a quantity word that matches the noun and sentence type.
a1-some-any-quantities.explain: Use some in many positive sentences: “We have some apples.” Use any in many questions and negatives: “Do you have any milk?” “We don't have any milk.” Use a few with countable plural nouns and a little with uncountable nouns. Use a lot of with both types.
a1-some-any-quantities.contrast: Some can also appear in an offer when you expect a positive answer: “Would you like some tea?” Use how many with countable plural nouns and how much with uncountable nouns. Check the noun before choosing the quantity word.
a1-some-any-quantities.example: We have a few tomatoes and a little rice, but we don't have any cheese.
a1-some-any-quantities.reason: Tomatoes can be counted, so the sentence uses a few. Rice and cheese are uncountable here.
a1-some-any-quantities.foundation: Quantity words depend on how the noun is counted. Identify the noun first, then choose the matching expression.

a1-superlatives.title: Superlatives
a1-superlatives.summary: Say which person or thing has the highest or lowest quality.
a1-superlatives.goal: Compare one person or thing with a whole group.
a1-superlatives.explain: Use a superlative to identify the highest or lowest degree in a group. Short adjectives often add -est: small/smallest. Long adjectives often use the most: the most comfortable. Use the before a superlative in common patterns: “the tallest building.” Some forms are irregular: good/best and bad/worst.
a1-superlatives.contrast: A comparative compares two items and often uses than. A superlative compares one item with a group: “This is the cheapest shop in town.” Do not use more and -est together. Name the group when it is not clear.
a1-superlatives.example: Of the three bags, this one is the lightest. It is also the most comfortable.
a1-superlatives.reason: Light uses -est. Comfortable uses the most because it is a longer adjective.
a1-superlatives.foundation: A superlative needs a group for comparison. Decide which items belong to the group before choosing the best or largest.

a1-there-was-were.title: There was and there were
a1-there-was-were.summary: Say what existed or was present in a place in the past.
a1-there-was-were.goal: Describe past places and things that existed there.
a1-there-was-were.explain: Use there was with one thing or an uncountable noun: “There was a shop.” Use there were with plural nouns: “There were two shops.” Use a past time phrase such as last year or yesterday. Make a negative with wasn't or weren't. Make a question by moving was or were before there.
a1-there-was-were.contrast: Use there was/were to introduce what existed. Use a name and was/were to describe a known place: “There was a café. The café was small.” Do not use did with there was/were questions.
a1-there-was-were.example: There was a park near my old house, but there weren't any shops.
a1-there-was-were.reason: A park is singular, so it takes was. Shops is plural, so it takes were.
a1-there-was-were.foundation: There was/were describes existence in the past. Choose was or were by the noun that follows.

a1-this-that-these-those.title: This, that, these and those
a1-this-that-these-those.summary: Point to objects and say whether they are near or far.
a1-this-that-these-those.goal: Identify people or things by distance and number.
a1-this-that-these-those.explain: Use this for one nearby thing and these for more than one nearby thing. Use that for one thing farther away and those for more than one farther away. Put the demonstrative before a noun: this book, those chairs. You can also use it alone: “Which one?” “This one.”
a1-this-that-these-those.contrast: This and that are singular, so use is or a singular noun. These and those are plural, so use are or a plural noun. Do not add a plural -s to the demonstrative itself.
a1-this-that-these-those.example: This cup is mine. Those cups are yours.
a1-this-that-these-those.reason: This points to one nearby cup. Those points to more than one cup farther away.
a1-this-that-these-those.foundation: Demonstratives combine two ideas: distance and number. Check both before choosing the word.

a1-transport-tickets.title: Transport and tickets
a1-transport-tickets.summary: Ask about routes, times and ticket prices.
a1-transport-tickets.goal: Buy a ticket and understand simple travel information.
a1-transport-tickets.explain: Use “Where does this bus go?” to ask about a route and “What time does it leave?” to ask about a schedule. Use at for an exact departure time and from/to for the start and end of a journey. Ask “How much is a ticket?” for the price. Use one-way and return to describe ticket types.
a1-transport-tickets.contrast: Timetables use the present simple for scheduled times: “The train leaves at six.” Use can I…? to make a polite request: “Can I have a return ticket?” Check the destination, time and number of tickets.
a1-transport-tickets.example: Can I have two return tickets to the city centre? What time does the next bus leave?
a1-transport-tickets.reason: Return describes the ticket type. What time asks for a scheduled departure.
a1-transport-tickets.foundation: When travelling, confirm three details: destination, time and ticket type. Repeat important numbers to avoid mistakes.

a1-weather-clothes.title: Weather and clothes
a1-weather-clothes.summary: Describe the weather and choose what to wear.
a1-weather-clothes.goal: Talk about today's weather and suitable clothes.
a1-weather-clothes.explain: Use it is + adjective to describe weather: “It's cold,” “It's sunny.” Use it is raining or it is snowing for weather happening now. Use wear for clothes: “I wear a coat in winter.” Use am/is/are wearing for clothes someone has on now: “She is wearing a blue jacket.”
a1-weather-clothes.contrast: Present simple describes a usual choice or season. Present continuous describes what is happening now or what someone is wearing at this moment. Use a before one countable item: a coat, an umbrella.
a1-weather-clothes.example: It's raining today, so I'm wearing a coat and carrying an umbrella.
a1-weather-clothes.reason: It's raining describes current weather. I'm wearing describes clothes now. So links the weather to the choice.
a1-weather-clothes.foundation: Weather language often links a condition with a practical choice. Describe the weather first, then say what clothing is suitable.

a1-work-introductions.title: Introducing yourself at work
a1-work-introductions.summary: Share your name, job, workplace and basic duties.
a1-work-introductions.goal: Give a simple work introduction and ask a colleague basic questions.
a1-work-introductions.explain: Use be to give your name, job or workplace: “I'm a driver.” Use the present simple to describe duties: “I deliver packages.” With he or she, add -s to the main verb: “She manages a team.” Use at before a company or workplace name in common phrases: “I work at a hotel.”
a1-work-introductions.contrast: A job title names a role; a present simple verb describes a regular task. Use “I am…” for a role and “I work…” for an activity or workplace. Ask “What do you do?” about a person's job.
a1-work-introductions.example: Hi, I'm Daniel. I'm a mechanic and I work at a garage near the station.
a1-work-introductions.reason: I'm a mechanic gives the job. I work at a garage gives the workplace.
a1-work-introductions.foundation: A clear introduction gives a name, role and one useful detail. Use short sentences and speak at a steady pace.
